questions.q: What does 'granularity' (or grain) mean for a table?
options: The level of detail a single row represents — e.g., one row per order vs. one row per customer
The total number of rows in the table
The number of columns in the table
Whether the table is a live connection or an extract
questions.explain: Granularity describes what one row means: an Orders table at one-row-per-order grain is finer than a Customers table at one-row-per-customer grain.

questions.q: If Customers (100 rows, one per customer) is joined to Orders (340 rows, one per order) on CustomerID, how many rows does the joined result have, and why?
options: 340 — each customer row is duplicated once for every matching order
100 — joins always keep the smaller table's row count
440 — joins always add the two row counts together
34,000 — joins always multiply the two row counts together
questions.explain: Each customer row repeats once per matching order row, so the joined result lands at 340 rows — the granularity of the finer (Orders) side.

questions.q: Why is a fan-out especially dangerous — what makes it hard to spot?
options: Every individual row in the joined result still looks completely correct — the mistake only shows up once you aggregate (SUM/COUNT)
It causes Tableau to throw a visible error message immediately
It only affects live connections, never extracts
It's impossible to happen if you're only using inner joins
questions.explain: Each joined row is individually accurate — the problem is a customer-level value getting summed once per order, which only becomes visible in an aggregate total.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why do relationships avoid the fan-out problem that joins can cause?
options: Relationships aggregate each side to the level of detail a worksheet actually needs before combining data, instead of combining rows immediately at the row level
Relationships physically delete duplicate rows from the source tables
Relationships can only be used with tables that have identical granularity
Relationships don't have this issue because they never combine data at all
questions.explain: A relationship defers and aggregates per worksheet, sidestepping fan-out. A join, like a SQL JOIN, combines immediately at the row level and inherits the same fan-out risk you'd get writing the SQL by hand.

questions.q: Which of these is a valid fix for a fan-out problem when you must use a join?
options: Pre-aggregate the 'many' side down to one row per key before joining, so both sides share a grain
Switch the join type from Inner to Full Outer
Add more join clauses to the same join
Rename the joined fields
questions.explain: Pre-aggregating the finer-grained side to match the other side's grain (or using a relationship, or an LOD expression) prevents the row multiplication that causes fan-out.
